src/rt/abort.cpp.note: Abort dispatch is synchronous, so callback reentrancy and ownership during dispatch are the relevant suspension-equivalent boundaries.

sites.label: Dependent signal registration and pinning
sites.reason: The source temporarily owns interested dependents, the reverse links are weak, and abort moves pins and promoted dependents outside the registry before dispatch.

sites.label: Listener snapshots and removal traversal
sites.reason: Dispatch owns a snapshot of unique entries plus the executing callback, and live-vector removal exits its traversal immediately.

sites.label: Abort dispatch borrows the controller's state slot
sites.reason: A synchronous listener may release or replace the controller that owns the shared pointer still used by the dispatch epilogue.

defect.severity: memory safety in the public runtime API
interleaving: AbortController::abort passes a reference to its own shared pointer and begins notifying listeners.
A listener drops the controller or replaces its signal. Dispatch then accesses the ended state or cleans up the replacement's listeners through that borrowed slot.

sites.label: onabort setter and getter in current dispatch paths
sites.reason: The handler slot and listener entry own callback copies and dispatch pins the active callable while assignment or removal changes the slot.

sites.label: AbortSignal timeout callback
sites.reason: The unreferenced timer owns the signal by value, the signal has no timer backedge, and firing or loop teardown releases the callback.

sites.label: Native cancellation bridge
sites.reason: The completion handler owns the cancellation slot and signal while the listener uses a weak signal link, and completion removes any surviving registration.

sites.label: Abortable sleep timer and listener
sites.reason: The timer and listener intentionally retain each other while armed, and abort, timeout, or loop teardown clears an owning callback before releasing the active invocation.

include/uos/rt/abort.hpp.note: The public header declares the abort bridge and listener handles. The implementation's reentrant dispatch defect is counted at its source.

sites.label: Listener identity and invocation
sites.reason: Each identity shares an owning function and the runtime dispatch copies the listener before invoking it, allowing deregistration during the call.

sites.label: Signal owner and borrowed accessors in current callers
sites.reason: The handle owns its state, callers copy or consume reason and state synchronously, and the separate abort-dispatch borrow is tracked in abort.cpp.

sites.label: Eager abortable wrapper
sites.reason: This ordinary function moves its Task into runInto and returns a Task owning the result state, while its fetch caller gives the native child owned request inputs.

src/rt/clock.cpp.note: Timer APIs are synchronous. The one Task-returning overload creates an owning result before handing it to the lazy awaiter.

sites.label: Timer queue ownership and disarm
sites.reason: The queue owns each entry and the timer has a weak queue backedge; handles retain their timer during synchronous dequeue and callback release.

sites.label: Self-replacement of injected global hooks
sites.reason: Current production uses defaults and the scoped fixture overrides checked retain their captures. Supporting an override that replaces its own slot while it runs would require proving an independent callable owner.

sites.label: Timeout handle operations
sites.reason: Ref, unref and refresh are synchronous, lock the weak queue locally, and do not publish a reference to the handle.

sites.label: Sleep callback and timer construction
sites.reason: The callback and awaiter independently own Promise state, and each newly queued timer owns its moved callback.

sites.label: Timer dispatch and callback rearm
sites.reason: The dispatcher pins the timer, erases the map entry and moves out the callable before invoking code that may clear or rearm it.

sites.label: Timer teardown
sites.reason: Teardown owns a detached map and releases moved callbacks after marking the corresponding timers disarmed.

include/uos/rt/clock.hpp.note: The injected Clock methods are synchronous. Loop's borrowed Clock dependency is assessed in async.cpp and async.hpp.

sites.label: Timeout timer ownership
sites.reason: Timeout is a shared handle and the implementation consumes its state accessor within synchronous timer operations.

sites.label: Timer registration and scheduling API
sites.reason: Registration accepts an owning callable by value, clearing borrows only synchronously, and sleep creates and owns its result independently of the caller.

src/rt/async.cpp.note: Read the complete loop implementation and the PromiseCore callbacks. The process loop is intentionally permanent. Scoped loops have an explicit teardown path.

sites.label: Loop owns the context and timer queue and borrows its Clock
sites.reason: A scoped Loop's clock is declared before it in the runtime fixture, and the permanent default Loop uses the static SystemClock.

sites.label: Asio executor's Loop implementation pointer
sites.reason: The Loop contract confines I/O and executor users to the owner lifetime, and execute owns dispatched handlers or discards them once the context is gone.

sites.label: Microtask callback dispatch
sites.reason: Each one-shot job is moved out before it can reenter the loop, and rejection candidates live in a detached vector while they are inspected.

sites.label: Intrusive Promise waiting-list mutation
sites.reason: Promise destruction unlinks synchronously, and teardown unlinks and pins each node before destroying its reactions and any continuations they own.

sites.label: Scoped Loop teardown runs callbacks under the ambient loop
sites.reason: A destroyed frame can queue a microtask from a ScopeExit while the dying loop is absent from currentLoop, letting that job survive in an unrelated loop.

defect.severity: wrong-loop teardown and retention
interleaving: A pending coroutine belongs to a local Loop. Loop::run or blockOn returns and its LoopScope restores the previous loop.
Destroying the local Loop drops the frame. A destructor that queues a cleanup job sends it to the previous or permanent process loop, outside the teardown drain.

sites.label: Run-loop stop predicate and scope guards
sites.reason: The synchronous caller holds the stop Promise through runLoop, and the local guards restore the running flag and scope before returning.

sites.label: Promise settlement traversal
sites.reason: Reactions move into the microtask queue without invocation during traversal, and unhandled rejections keep a separate shared owner until the checkpoint.

sites.label: Native start and user microtask registration
sites.reason: Asio owns the moved task and a captureless completion handler, and the queue owns the moved user callable.

sites.label: Parked awaiter and pending Promise ownership
sites.reason: The waiter job owns the coroutine that owns the Promise; settlement and loop teardown break the cycle. Identifying indefinitely abandoned request waiters would establish where this topology retains request state on the permanent loop.

sites.label: Waker, abandon and microtask initiations
sites.reason: Each initiation is named and synchronous, and the handler goes to a weakly linked slot, to the loop, or is intentionally discarded.

sites.label: Pending Promise reactions self-own their source
sites.reason: A dropped never-settled input keeps its reaction and combinator output alive until Loop destruction, including losers of a completed combination on the permanent loop.

defect.severity: retention on long-running loops
interleaving: all registers a reaction whose owning source capture points to the state storing that reaction. Another input can reject the combined Promise.
Drop the pending input and every resolver. Its last ownership is the reaction inside itself, so neither that source nor the captured output/continuations can be reclaimed.

include/uos/rt/async.hpp.note: Reviewed the lazy Task adapters, eager Promise combinators, callback return-type branches and generator implementation. The Promise callback defect is reachable through the public API. The production continuations checked consume by-reference inputs synchronously or use owned values.

sites.label: One-shot jobs and waiting-list declarations
sites.reason: Job moves its erased callable into a local before invocation, and the intrusive list is maintained and unlinked synchronously by the loop implementation.

sites.label: Owned awaiters and public Promise accessors
sites.reason: The wrappers synchronously copy the state or move the task into an owning frame, while value, reason and state accessors borrow from a live Promise in the checked callers.

sites.label: Implicit shared_ptr conversion in Promise await expressions
sites.reason: Both awaiters form a shared_ptr<PromiseCore> temporary from a typed shared_ptr in the await full expression.

defect.severity: GCC 12 portability rule
interleaving: awaitOwned or awaitState calls awaitSettled directly with a typed state. The call converts it to an owning base shared_ptr inside co_await.
The retained GCC 12 coroutine rule rejects this expression shape because await temporaries can be destroyed twice. This occurrence has static evidence.

sites.label: Loop, Clock, Scope and blockOn borrowed API
sites.reason: The synchronous blockOn owns its stop Promise and the current-loop scope is nested inside the named Loop and Clock lifetimes in the checked callers.

sites.label: Synchronous resolver and detached-task entry points
sites.reason: Resolvers share their state, newPromise calls its executor synchronously, and spawn hands the Task to runInto; a Task's own borrowed inputs remain governed by its caller.

sites.label: Coroutine holders and finally helpers
sites.reason: callHeld, keepAlive and withFinally keep the callback or explicit owner in an awaited frame; ScopeExit owns its synchronous cleanup and the helpers use named results.

sites.label: Task-returning Promise callbacks can borrow a destroyed outcome
sites.reason: The Task-keeping branch pins the callable, but a coroutine parameter referencing the fulfilled value or rejection reason still borrows the source state held only by the reaction.

defect.severity: memory safety in the public runtime API
interleaving: Register a then or catch callback whose Task takes a const reference to the outcome. Drop the source Promise while keeping the derived Promise.
The queued reaction starts the callback until its first suspension. The reaction finishes and releases the source, then the callback resumes with a dangling outcome reference.

sites.label: Typed Promise reactions retain pending sources and input tuples
sites.reason: These registrations repeat the self-owning reaction pattern. Apply the source ownership handoff in the ranked fix and collect fulfilled tuple slots without retaining the tuple of input Promises.

sites.label: finally_ callable and settled source access
sites.reason: The synchronous branch reads the source inside its reaction, and the Task branch retains the callable through completion and the source through the after reaction.

sites.label: Combinator storage and traversal across sibling completion
sites.reason: Registered reactions are synchronous and own their result storage and copied indices, so sibling completion cannot invalidate a borrowed iterator or closure.

sites.label: Generator queue dispatch
sites.reason: A request is moved out before delivery, the launch callable is moved out before execution, and queued work promotes a weak core only for synchronous mutation.

sites.label: Generator yield and weak waker parking
sites.reason: The Yield task owns its value and holds a weak backedge while parked, and Waker moves the current waiter out before resuming it.

sites.label: Generator body and yielding adapters
sites.reason: The body closure and return slot move into runGenerator's frame, and the public Yield wrappers take a value or copy the weak handle before returning a Task.

sites.label: Pending generator step does not keep its generator alive
sites.reason: A returned next or return Task owns only the result, so dropping the last generator handle while the body is executing can strand an outstanding step.

defect.severity: public runtime liveness
interleaving: Call next on a generator whose body first yields through a microtask. Keep the step Task and release the generator handle before that microtask runs.
yieldTo finds the weak core expired and abandons the body. The outstanding step has no owner capable of fulfilling or rejecting it.

sites.label: Delegate and forAwait ownership
sites.reason: The frames own both generator handles or callback and the complete current IteratorResult through the body await and return cleanup.

sites.label: Forwarded generator values constructed within await expressions
sites.reason: delegateTo moves a yielded T into a by-value adapter and forAwait may move it into a by-value coroutine callback in the await full expression.

defect.severity: GCC 12 portability rule
interleaving: Instantiate the forwarding helpers with an owning yielded value, such as bytes, and a by-value callback. The moved parameter is materialized in the await expression.
The retained GCC 12 coroutine rules require creating that operation in a separate statement. This occurrence has static evidence.

src/rt/process_loop.cpp.note: Reviewed both pidfd and SIGCHLD branches, subprocess pipe streams, process listeners and BunFile stream adapters. The production server registers process signals on the process loop.

sites.label: POSIX child exit wait and signal names
sites.reason: The watcher owns its signal_set and PID throughout the wait, the error token is named, and Darwin's string views point into static storage.

sites.label: Static process signal registry retains a scoped Asio context
sites.reason: A listener registered on a scoped Loop can leave a static signal_set whose service and executor have already died.

defect.severity: memory safety with scoped runtime loops
interleaving: Register process::on inside a local LoopScope. The static signal registry constructs its Asio signal_set on that loop.
Destroy the loop before explicitly removing the listener. Later registry use or destruction still uses the old Asio service and executor.

sites.label: Signal wait generation and synchronous listener dispatch
sites.reason: The wait callback captures a generation by value; listener delivery snapshots owning identities and erases once entries before invoking any callback.

sites.label: Subprocess pipe read and cancellation
sites.reason: The source closures own the descriptor, the forwarding pull moves an owned controller into the child frame, and the frame owns its I/O buffer and token through completion.

sites.label: FileSink input views and suspended flush
sites.reason: write synchronously copies incoming views, and each flush owns the stable descriptor via its state and the moved chunk independently of later changes to pending.

sites.label: Child-exit observers and public subprocess accessors
sites.reason: The watchers own state and native descriptors across waits, while accessors synchronously copy owning handles and kill consumes its view before returning.

sites.label: Spawn setup and watcher detachment
sites.reason: The borrowing lambdas and argv or env pointers are synchronous, and the detached watchers receive state and their native wait inputs by value.

sites.label: BunFile stream callbacks and descriptor lifetime
sites.reason: The source owns its pathname and descriptor, the synchronous pull and cancel closures own that source, and close clears the fd before teardown.

include/uos/rt/process.hpp.note: The ProcessLoop public interface is split from its implementation in process_loop.cpp and the loop-free functions in process.cpp.

sites.label: Signal Listener closure and signal-name views
sites.reason: Registration copies the owning Listener identity, delivery invokes an owned snapshot, and the event/name views are used synchronously or point to static signal-name strings.

sites.label: FileSink and Subprocess handle APIs
sites.reason: Writes and kill consume their views synchronously, and deferred work gets shared state from the handle or returns an owning stream or Promise copy.

sites.label: BunFile path and stream declaration
sites.reason: The object owns its path and stream copies that path into the source before returning, allowing the BunFile wrapper to be a temporary.

src/rt/stream.cpp.note: This translation unit contains synchronous reason/value construction and explicit ByteChunk template instantiations. The instantiated suspension sites are recorded in stream.hpp.

sites.label: Tee cancellation reason construction
sites.reason: The helpers consume the borrowed exception handles synchronously and the resulting exception owns both reasons and its JSON representation.

include/uos/rt/stream.hpp.note: Reviewed eager reader registration, source callback type erasure, reentrant cancellation, branch teeing and generator adapters. A copied controller is a strong stream owner. A copy kept in closure-owned state therefore needs an independent release path.

sites.label: Source algorithm callable lifetime
sites.reason: The start source is owned by the constructor, runtime pull/cancel calls use local algorithm copies and runAsync retains the erased coroutine closure throughout each asynchronous call.

sites.label: Borrowing callback parameters through the by-value erased signature
sites.reason: The current callbacks checked take owned values or complete synchronously. A supported ABI check with a Task callback taking const A& would establish whether the materialized std::function parameter survives throughout its await.

sites.label: Stream callback and yield arguments materialized inside awaits
sites.reason: runAsync forwards an owning erased argument and iterateStream moves an owning chunk within the await full expressions.

defect.severity: GCC 12 portability rule
interleaving: A stream uses an owning controller, cancellation reason or chunk in a callback/yield invocation. The argument is materialized inside co_await.
The GCC 12 rule calls for creating the Task separately. Using an rvalue-reference erased signature keeps a borrowing callee attached to runAsync's frame while performing that split.

sites.label: Controller and active pull ownership
sites.reason: The executing controller and pull reaction pin state during use; a callback-owned controller cache can create a separate persistent backedge, assessed at each such source.

sites.label: Stream reactions capture their own pending Promise states
sites.reason: The pull, cancel, start and tee closed callbacks repeat the pending-source cycle from PromiseCore. Their source states need ownership only during delivery.

sites.label: Stream and reader queue drain boundaries
sites.reason: Chunk and reader-request entries are moved out before settlement, reader release pins the stream, and Promise settlement queues reactions outside these synchronous traversals.

sites.label: Read registration and reader accessors
sites.reason: Read registration happens synchronously and returns an owned result state, and no borrow of the reader's stream is used after a pull callback can reenter.

sites.label: Stream cancel borrows the owner slot through callback invocation
sites.reason: The callback can release the reader or replace the stream handle while the cancellation epilogue still dereferences its shared_ptr slot.

defect.severity: memory safety in stream cancellation
interleaving: reader.cancel closes the stream and invokes the underlying cancel callback while borrowing reader->stream.
The callback releases the reader lock. The same shared_ptr slot becomes null, then cancelStreamInto dereferences it to clear the algorithms.

sites.label: In-flight tee read keeps abandoned branches' source alive
sites.reason: Weak branch references avoid one direct backedge, while an unfulfilled source read still owns the teeRead continuation that owns the source through TeeState.

defect.severity: retention on cloned streaming bodies
interleaving: Tee starts a read of a source that has no next chunk yet, registering the continuation on the source read request.
Drop both branch handles and the original source. The read request owns the parked frame, whose TeeState parameter owns the source and its read queue until external settlement or Loop teardown.

sites.label: Tee cancellation releases its tee owner before waiting
sites.reason: The cancel coroutine transfers to the shared completion state once branch bookkeeping is done, and adoption owns the source cancellation operation.

sites.label: Tee cancellation converts the shared Promise state inside the await
sites.reason: The typed shared_ptr is converted to a base shared_ptr in the co_await full expression. Use the same named Task as for awaitOwned.

sites.label: Tee delivery and stream iterator step storage
sites.reason: The current step belongs to the coroutine, promoted branch handles are local, and the iteration frame owns its reader while it awaits the stored read or cancel.

src/rt/http.cpp.note: Read the body readers and stream adapters, clone/transfer paths, synchronous FormData parsing and static MIME data. This file models Fetch values. The server transport lives outside Area A.

sites.label: Blob data and temporary Blob handles
sites.reason: The ordinary member wrappers copy the shared immutable bytes into the coroutine or stream before the receiver can die.

sites.label: Buffered body streams and their source callbacks
sites.reason: The source owns bytes and offset without a stream backedge, and the copied pull algorithm owns both for synchronous iteration and close.

sites.label: FormData parse, serialize and entry mutation views
sites.reason: All parser views and entry iterators are consumed synchronously under the owned body or FormData and the products own their bytes and strings.

sites.label: Body extraction, clone, header and transfer wrappers
sites.reason: The reference captures are invoked immediately by visit and body cloning transfers owning stream handles synchronously. Tee retention is tracked at its implementation.

sites.label: Request and Response read tasks and their inputs
sites.reason: The wrappers snapshot owned data or a reader before returning, and each frame owns the read operation, complete step, accumulated bytes and form boundary during later awaits.

sites.label: Abandoned streamed-body reader lock
sites.reason: The eager wrapper locks the body before the lazy Task starts and release is reached on success. Decide the required lock and cancellation behavior when a caller discards an unstarted Task or a stream read rejects, then exercise that behavior with an independently retained body handle.

include/uos/rt/http.hpp.note: Reviewed the Blob, File, FormData, Request and Response API. The public Task methods are ordinary entry points that acquire ownership before the corresponding implementation coroutine starts.

sites.label: Blob and File construction, getters and asynchronous reads
sites.reason: Value construction consumes views synchronously, borrowed getters refer to the owning handle, and asynchronous reads copy the backing shared_ptr at call time.

sites.label: FormData borrowed entries and iterators
sites.reason: Mutators and accessors execute synchronously. The reader and serializer paths finish entry traversal before returning or suspending.

sites.label: Response handle and body methods
sites.reason: Response owns shared state, reference getters are synchronous in the checked callers, and the body adapters return tasks with independently owned inputs.

sites.label: Request construction, body APIs and transfer
sites.reason: The constructors consume URL and init borrows synchronously, property access borrows a live handle, and each deferred body reader takes owned state from the ordinary wrapper.

include/uos/rt/fetch.hpp.note: The statically erased Fetch and MockTransport callback signatures are the ownership boundary. Current callers mostly use by-value callback inputs. The generic Fetch constructor also accepts reference-taking coroutine callables.

sites.label: Ordinary Fetch wrapping and scoped global overrides
sites.reason: The synchronous Response wrapper captures its callable by shared owner and returns a value-owning Task, and an override owns its copied predecessor.

sites.label: Fetch erasure can discard input storage before a borrowing coroutine starts
sites.reason: The invocability constraint accepts reference-taking callables, but the by-value erased invocation can destroy its RequestInfo and RequestInit before their borrowed uses.

defect.severity: memory safety in the injectable Fetch API
interleaving: Construct Fetch with a coroutine callable taking const RequestInfo& or const RequestInit&. Fetch invokes the by-value std::function and returns a lazy Task.
The full expression in Fetch::operator() ends and destroys the erased argument. The child resumes with a dangling reference even though keepAlive retains the callable.

sites.label: Transport input and recorded request views
sites.reason: The virtual request parameter owns a handle and the recorded vector view is consumed while the MockTransport is held. The lifetime of the virtual receiver and callback is assessed at their implementations.

include/uos/rt/fetch_transport.hpp.note: Reviewed the options and transport interface. The implementation copies the shared client state at the public send boundary, and the scoped-loop disposal path is covered at Pool.

sites.label: Client options, send wrapper and installation
sites.reason: Options and requests cross entry points by value, deferred send takes a shared ClientState, and synchronous pool access and global installation use owning transport handles.

include/uos/rt/gzip.hpp.note: The incremental codec interface exposes synchronous borrows with explicit validity windows. The coroutine wrappers take Bytes by value.

sites.label: Inflater input and output spans in gateway callers
sites.reason: The fetch decoder drains and copies each inflater piece synchronously while the calling buffer and unique codec state remain alive.

sites.label: One-shot, callback and coroutine codec APIs
sites.reason: The piece callback runs synchronously before the borrowed span changes and both Task APIs own their bytes across the microtask.

include/uos/rt/websocket.hpp.note: Reviewed the listener and callback shapes, client and server ownership contracts and the upgrade handoff. Event views and target pointers are call-scoped in the checked production handlers.

sites.label: Incoming values and event borrows in the checked callers
sites.reason: The native dispatch owns the active event, gateway listeners consume its raw pointers synchronously, and scheduled work copies payload or response data first.

sites.label: Listener identity and declared EventEmitter storage
sites.reason: The emitter owns the registered functions and dispatch uses owning snapshot entries. This pins callable identity through reentrant listener removal.

sites.label: Client construction, send callbacks and event attributes
sites.reason: Asynchronous sends transfer owning payload and callable values, and attribute wrappers belong to the socket's registry. Receiver ownership during delivery is assessed in the implementation.

sites.label: Self-replacement of injected buffered-amount getter
sites.reason: The production getter is fixed. Supporting a configured getter that overwrites its own callable requires testing that invocation with an independently pinned callable.

sites.label: Upgrade API borrows and cross-loop ownership
sites.reason: Protocol and upgrade callbacks run synchronously against the caller's request, the socket is moved into native state, and client list access returns an owning vector snapshot.

src/rt/fetch.cpp.note: Reviewed both request-init paths, both abort windows, the transport seam and the replaceable global Fetch slot. The installed HTTP client has an owning send wrapper. The polymorphic transport API also permits coroutine member implementations.

sites.label: Request preparation and forwarding into owned tasks
sites.reason: The validation wrappers are synchronous, variant references end before dispatch, and rejected or sending tasks take owned reasons or Request handles.

sites.label: Response abort and cancel delivery while active
sites.reason: The callback promotes a weak body for the whole invocation, pull and cancel frames own their parameters, and detached reader cancellation has an owned result independent of its caller.

sites.label: Dropped abortable response body is kept by its own controller
sites.reason: The wrapper's algorithms own AbortableBody and AbortableBody owns the controller of that same stream. Normal completion clears the algorithms but an unread HWM-zero response may be abandoned without a terminal callback.

defect.severity: request-path leak
interleaving: A request with an explicit signal receives a streaming response. The front end caches the wrapper's controller in the owner retained by its pull and cancel callbacks.
The caller drops the response without reading it or aborting. No pull occurs, and the controller, stream algorithms, source reader and signal remain retained.

sites.label: Abort can outlive the owning virtual transport frame
sites.reason: The default HTTP client copies ClientState before suspension. A transport whose member coroutine uses its receiver can survive the front-end await without owning the virtual object.

defect.severity: memory safety in the injectable transport path
interleaving: An installed transport's member send coroutine suspends on an rt Promise. Replace the global transport so sendThrough is its remaining owner, then abort the signal.
abortable rejects sendThrough immediately but cannot interrupt the rt Promise. sendThrough releases the transport while the child's member frame remains pending.

sites.label: Abort-window result and owned error callback
sites.reason: The send frame owns the signal and response and schedules a source with its own Reason. The wrapper uses synchronous factories and the awaited abortable Task is named.

sites.label: Fetch calls a replaceable slot before reliably taking ownership
sites.reason: Argument evaluation may invoke the old callable before copying its owner. A synchronous injected function can replace the active slot and drop its own closure during that invocation.

defect.severity: memory safety during a reentrant Fetch callback
interleaving: fetch invokes a synchronous Fetch callback through the global slot. The callable argument to keepAlive is evaluated first and the callback replaces globalThis.fetch.
Replacement drops the callback's only owner. Its remaining code or returned child can borrow the destroyed closure, and keepAlive can pick up the replacement.

sites.label: Injected async Fetch arguments cross the erasure lifetime boundary
sites.reason: The wrapper retains the callable but the by-value std::function invocation owns its arguments only within that call expression.

sites.label: Mock transport returns a callback task without its handler owner
sites.reason: The ordinary send method records a copy but passes a separate erased Request to its handler and returns the child task directly.

defect.severity: memory safety in local transport injection
interleaving: Call MockTransport::send with a capturing coroutine handler and release the mock while retaining the returned task.
The lazy handler then runs with a dangling closure. A handler borrowing the erased Request also loses that argument at the end of send's call expression.

src/rt/fetch_transport.cpp.note: Reviewed DNS, both connection branches, concurrent upload/download, stale retry, redirects, EOF/error/cancel and pooling handoff. The writer starts independently so an early response can be delivered before upload completion.

sites.label: Owned request body and DNS inputs
sites.reason: The request frame owns both handles and copies bytes. The resolver frame owns host, service, resolver, error token and the final endpoint copy.

sites.label: DNS cancellation closure
sites.reason: The cancellation slot retains only a weak resolver reference, and the active resolution keeps the resolver and slot context alive until completion or teardown.

sites.label: TCP connection, TLS receiver and pool acquisition
sites.reason: The private endpoint vector cannot be mutated by other work, and the connecting frame owns the client, TLS context owner and Connection across the handshake.

sites.label: Detached write task, dynamic buffers and local cleanup
sites.reason: The writer owns connection, reader, upload inputs and each write owner. The synchronous scope-exit reference is to a local declared before its guard.

sites.label: Terminal connection close can strand a detached upload reader
sites.reason: Closing the socket wakes its native operations. A writeRequest frame waiting on a JavaScript-style reader Promise also needs its reader released or cancelled.

defect.severity: request-path retention after a failed or early response
interleaving: The client sends the upload head and parks its detached writer in reader.read(). The peer closes before the response head, or the early response finishes before the upload source produces another chunk.
The terminal exchange closes the socket with an unaborted signal. The upload Promise never settles and retains the writer, stream and closed connection on the process loop.

sites.label: Exchange head parse, retry and connection handoff
sites.reason: Response head fields are owned and the input view ends before fill; retry passes owned configuration and connection into the exchange frame.

sites.label: Response pump, parser views and source closures
sites.reason: The stream owns the pump while active, pool backedges are weak, and parser views are consumed before queue mutation or suspension. Scope-bound loop ownership is required by docs/rt/async.md.

sites.label: Native fill receiver during response cancellation
sites.reason: The named fill Task pins the Connection through the native read. Cancellation sets the shared flag before dropping the pump's slot, and the continuation checks it before using that slot.

sites.label: Post-head upload failure leaves a response read parked
sites.reason: The detached upload writer can close the Connection with a body failure after the response exists. The response pull treats the resulting aborted read as a silent successful pull.

defect.severity: request-path pending response read
interleaving: The response head arrives while an upload and a response body read are both pending. The upload reader rejects and writeRequest records the failure and closes the connection.
The body fill reports aborted with pump.cancelled false. pullBody returns without closing or erroring the stream, leaving the downstream reader Promise and its continuation parked.

sites.label: Redirect drain, header edits and public send owner
sites.reason: The redirect frame owns request metadata, next URL and exchange. Header iteration is synchronous, and the public ordinary wrapper copies ClientState into the deferred operation.

src/rt/fetch_transport_codec.cpp.note: Reviewed native and dynamically resolved codec branches. Decoder operations and function-table initialization run synchronously.

sites.label: Zlib adapter and borrowed decoder buffers
sites.reason: The response pump owns the decoder and input during the synchronous write, and each inflater output span is copied before the next read. On failure the pump stops using the decoder.

sites.label: Brotli function table and streaming buffer ownership
sites.reason: Each decoder owns its C state and borrows a static API table, backed by the process-lifetime loader handle in the fallback. The C call uses stack buffers whose bytes are appended before returning.

sites.label: Zstd function table and streaming buffer ownership
sites.reason: Each decoder frees its C stream through the static API table; its input view and output buffer descriptors are used entirely in one synchronous write.

sites.label: Decoder selection and coding-name views
sites.reason: The code copies each view into its local vector before taking the selected reference, performs no later mutation of that vector and passes the URL into an owning string.

src/rt/fetch_transport_http.cpp.note: Reviewed the complete HTTP wire helpers, including incomplete and malformed parser returns. These helpers operate synchronously on caller-owned buffers.

sites.label: Header token views and error construction
sites.reason: Trim, token and line-parser views are consumed within the active caller, and FetchError takes value copies of the code and URL.

sites.label: Request field visits and sorting comparator
sites.reason: The header read, local vector sort and output assembly all run synchronously. The captureless comparator uses its arguments only within the sort.

sites.label: Connection token views into copied field strings
sites.reason: The outer range-for owns the temporary values vector for the loop's lifetime, and the inner token views are read before its current string can disappear.

sites.label: Response head parser input and output
sites.reason: Reason, name and value views borrow the caller's unmodified buffer during parsing; returned fields and reason own their strings.

sites.label: Framing token traversal and incremental chunk decode
sites.reason: Transfer-coding views borrow the immutable head during a synchronous scan, and the chunk decoder copies payload bytes before returning its status and offset.

sites.label: Byte queue compaction and caller views
sites.reason: Current exchange and pull callers consume or copy views before queue mutation or native I/O, and the native append sources are separate owned read buffers.

src/rt/fetch_transport_internal.hpp.note: Reviewed the internal transport declarations against their call sites and the Asio execution-context shutdown path.

sites.label: Synchronous parser, codec and byte queue interfaces
sites.reason: Parser and codec callers use borrowed views within the current operation, and their returned protocol values and appended buffers own their storage.

sites.label: Native connection tasks and receiver contract
sites.reason: Connect pins the receiver and ClientState for handshake, fill wraps its child with shared ownership, and the detached writer owns the connection and passes a separate buffer owner.

sites.label: Pool slots and Asio service ownership
sites.reason: The context owns the registry, whose map holds the pools. Slot references are synchronous, the timer captures a weak pool, and registry shutdown releases map owners before service destruction.

sites.label: Client per-loop registry observers and send inputs
sites.reason: The client uses the registry pointer only while a pool on that loop can be promoted. Current strong pool copies stay within synchronous code or a coroutine handled by the same context.

src/rt/fetch_transport_net.cpp.note: Reviewed the TCP and TLS paths, cancellation, idle timers, pool slots, registry teardown and both TLS context ownership modes.

sites.label: Connection idle timer and close
sites.reason: The registered timer holds a weak connection, promotes it only for synchronous close, and is disarmed by close or destruction.

sites.label: Handshake receiver, TLS context and read buffer
sites.reason: Connect owns the connection and client until handshake finishes, SSL takes the two BIOs, and the peer certificate reference is released synchronously after checking identity.

sites.label: Plain and TLS fill buffer owners
sites.reason: The fill wrapper pins its receiver even when cancellation clears the pump slot. Only the active response reader mutates the receiver's read buffer and input queue.

sites.label: Native write buffers through socket completion
sites.reason: The uploader owns the connection and the write frame owns its byte-buffer token. TLS flush copies ciphertext into its own vector before each write.

sites.label: Inline Asio buffer construction in native awaits
sites.reason: The awaits embed a constructed buffer descriptor. The port rule requires naming it before the await; current Clang compilation and the descriptor's trivial destruction do not demonstrate a GCC 12 failure.

defect.severity: GCC 12 portability rule
interleaving: The handshake, read or write initiates an Asio operation with an inline buffer descriptor inside the awaited expression.
The expression has the construction shape forbidden by the port. Separate the descriptor from the await on both connection branches.

sites.label: Idle connection probe and slot handoff
sites.reason: Pool scanning stays synchronous, moves a connection into a local owner before checking it, and only returns idle sockets whose upload and parser phase has ended.

sites.label: Pool timer reschedule and close traversal
sites.reason: The loop owns the timer job, the job temporarily promotes a weak pool, and no vector slot is borrowed across suspension or user callback invocation.

sites.label: Registry and TLS context lifetime during client teardown
sites.reason: Asio releases registry pool owners during service shutdown. The only other current pool owners are synchronous handles or same-context tasks destroyed before service deallocation, and the client and SSL connections hold their own context references.

src/rt/gzip.cpp.note: Reviewed the native and dynamically loaded zlib paths, incremental borrowed buffers, synchronous visitor delivery and the two Task wrappers.

sites.label: Zlib callback table across test seam replacement
sites.reason: An existing inflater holds a pointer to a static or list-owned table. Repointing the lookup slot preserves the old list node and its open library mapping.

sites.label: Allocator callback storage and output spans
sites.reason: Zlib registers stateless allocation functions and each allocated block owns its size header. Output spans are consumed synchronously before the next growth or transfer.

sites.label: Incremental inflater state and documented span borrows
sites.reason: The nonmovable heap state stays stable when the public handle moves. Checked callers keep input alive until drained, consume the current output span before another operation and stop on error.

sites.label: Synchronous compressor cleanup and piece visitor
sites.reason: The scope guard runs with its stream and static API still alive. The visitor runs synchronously, and the production and fixture callbacks copy each piece before the next inflater read.

sites.label: Compression and decompression Task frames
sites.reason: Each frame owns the input and result. Its noncoroutine scrub guard borrows the frame's input, and only the captureless zero-argument microtask runs after the codec work.

src/rt/tls.cpp.note: Read the trust-store setup, native ASN.1 ownership, hostname matching and C API callers. These routines do not suspend.

sites.label: File, ASN.1 and certificate-name views
sites.reason: The file stays open for the iterator copy, the certificate owner outlives synchronous extraction, and hostname matching reads unchanged local string vectors.

sites.label: Trust store and in-memory PEM ownership
sites.reason: The caller's PEM string stays alive until BIO_free, the store retains its certificate references, and the default context and its trust store are process-owned.

sites.label: OpenSSL name extraction and result copies
sites.reason: The names list and caller-owned certificate support the synchronous reads, while DNS names, IP addresses, error text and the returned reason are copied into owning strings or vectors.

src/rt/tls_internal.hpp.note: Checked the shared TLS declarations against Fetch and WebSocket callers in both context modes.

sites.label: TLS helper API and ownership handoff
sites.reason: The context accessors document whether callers receive ownership. The remaining declarations borrow their inputs only synchronously and return owned result values.

src/rt/websocket.cpp.note: Reviewed live and teardown ownership for client and server sockets, synchronous emitter reentrancy, and the native gateway upgrade caller. This file contains no coroutine bodies.

sites.label: Weak registry and listener teardown
sites.reason: The Asio service tracks weak identities. Shutdown moves the registry before promotion and pins each WebSocket locally while clearing listener cycles.

sites.label: A retained WebSocket outlives its Asio socket service
sites.reason: The service closes native handles and clears callbacks during shutdown, while the public WebSocket and its Sender still own the Asio socket object.

defect.severity: memory safety when a socket survives a scoped Loop
interleaving: Retain an opened or already-closed client WebSocket outside a scoped Loop. During context shutdown the registry closes its descriptor, while state.socket and Sender still hold the Asio object.
Destroy the last public WebSocket after the Loop. Its Asio socket destructor reaches the service destroyed with the old io_context.

sites.label: HTTP handshake and byte or string views
sites.reason: Header lookup and protocol parsing consume borrowed storage synchronously and copy it into owning results before an upgrade or deferred operation.

sites.label: Listener identity under mutation during delivery
sites.reason: The snapshot retains callbacks and fired flags while once removal and ordinary registration mutations affect only the live registry. Native delivery pins the receiver separately.

sites.label: Public event delivery can lose its WebSocket receiver
sites.reason: Direct emit through the public EventEmitter API has no owner to pin the derived WebSocket throughout snapshot iteration.

defect.severity: memory safety in explicit WebSocket event delivery
interleaving: Invoke public emit on a shared WebSocket and let its first listener reset the last external owner. The dispatch snapshot keeps callable identities alive.
The next once registration accesses the destroyed registry, or an attribute wrapper uses the deleted WebSocket as its target.

sites.label: Synchronous dispatch adapters and deferred post-close send result
sites.reason: Native event dispatch is reached through an owning WebSocket handle, stack event arguments stay local, and the posted send result captures its callback and reason by value.

sites.label: Close timer and receiver finish ownership
sites.reason: The close timer owns its native socket, and close detaches the timer and drains the receiver finish callback. Final delivery or registry teardown clears the remaining listener owners.

sites.label: Receiver and transport callback graph
sites.reason: Receiver hooks promote weak WebSocket links. Native transport hooks keep the public socket alive until close or loop teardown, and each dispatched onData consumes its bytes while the handler owns the buffer.

sites.label: Handshake abort and construction ownership
sites.reason: The connecting caller pins the WebSocket, abort clears request registrations synchronously, and pending close/error notifications own the WebSocket through dispatch.

sites.label: Injected buffered-amount getter replaces itself
sites.reason: The production getter is stable. The supported test override would need an explicit receiver/callable ownership rule or confirmation for reentrant self-replacement.

sites.label: Public writes and close-frame completion
sites.reason: The Sender materializes write bytes synchronously. Close's completion promotes a weak socket before accessing state, and native close is scheduled with an owning Socket handler.

sites.label: Attribute wrapper capture and replacement in native dispatch
sites.reason: The listener snapshot owns the callable while the native dispatch retains its WebSocket target. Direct public emit has the separate receiver pinning issue.

sites.label: Rejected upgrade response ownership
sites.reason: The native Socket takes the moved stream and owns pending writes, while the finish hook uses a weak backedge and the response bytes leave their local string before dispatch.

sites.label: Upgrade hooks can release the last WebSocketServer owner
sites.reason: The server method calls external factory, protocol and headers hooks before reusing its own options and client list. The gateway's named upgradeServer retains it, while the public method borrows its receiver.

defect.severity: memory safety in the public server upgrade API
interleaving: Call handleUpgrade using the last shared Server handle. A synchronous configured hook or headers listener drops that handle before returning.
completeUpgrade resumes and reads options_ or mutates clients_ after the server was destroyed.

sites.label: Upgrade inputs and tracked-client close
sites.reason: The gateway owns request and socket inputs through synchronous delivery. The tracking callback uses weak links, erases a client before posting the retained server's close notification, and leaves no client iterator suspended.

src/rt/websocket_client.cpp.note: Reviewed Unix and TCP resolve/connect paths, TLS callbacks, HTTP response parsing, and the opening handshake's success, failure, cancellation and unexpected-response branches. This translation unit has no coroutine bodies.

sites.label: Synchronous header and response parser borrows
sites.reason: All input views and container iterators remain inside the parser or builder. ParsedResponse owns the copied header values passed to callbacks.

sites.label: Opening timeout registration
sites.reason: The timer hook promotes a weak request and copies the current listener for its call. The request clears its timer on abort, error and completion.

sites.label: Unix-domain connect and cancellation
sites.reason: The Asio completion owns the request and Unix socket, and the independent cancellation hook owns the same socket until completion or abort clears it.

sites.label: TCP resolve, retry and socket handoff
sites.reason: Each operation holds the request and its socket or resolver, endpoints are copied into its completion, and the retry callable has a weak self-edge cleared on terminal completion.

sites.label: Connected socket and TLS callback ownership
sites.reason: The request owns its socket and each hook promotes a weak request for the synchronous call. The TLS handoff and socket write transfer values before their callbacks can run.

sites.label: Response upgrade, failure and abort cleanup
sites.reason: The parser copies any surplus bytes, then copies the active callback before clearing the registration. Abort moves the cancellation callable out before calling it.

sites.label: Unfinished ownership after a handled unexpected response
sites.reason: A registered unexpected-response listener takes the path that leaves request listeners installed until the connection closes. The listener contract needs to establish who must close a persistent response, including a listener that throws or retains no client handle.

sites.label: Client initialization and handshake listener arguments
sites.reason: Request construction copies local options and headers. Handshake callbacks own response, socket and key values, and their public WebSocket backedge is released on normal abort, close, error or upgrade, or registry shutdown.

src/rt/websocket_frame.cpp.note: Reviewed synchronous receiver parsing, event delivery, receiver error and finish notifications, and all Sender frame construction. There are no coroutine bodies in this translation unit.

sites.label: Receiver input and parser views
sites.reason: Socket supplies bytes to a synchronous copy, and each parse view is consumed before deferred error reporting or dispatch of a callback that could change the receiver.

sites.label: Completed message and control-frame delivery
sites.reason: The parser moves fragment storage out before calling listeners, passes owned event bytes and invokes an owning callable copy while the native dispatch retains the receiver.

sites.label: Receiver error and finish microtasks
sites.reason: The posted callbacks retain the receiver and copy each hook before invoking it. Close and registry shutdown clear the receiver's stored hooks.

sites.label: Sender frame assembly and data borrows
sites.reason: The frame serializes into owned bytes before its stack header and caller data can expire. Fragment bookkeeping is synchronous and precedes the socket write.

sites.label: Sender-to-socket ownership handoff
sites.reason: Sender holds the socket, and write receives owning frame bytes and a moved callback. The native write buffer lifetime is assessed in websocket_socket.cpp.

src/rt/websocket_internal.hpp.note: Reviewed internal callback declarations, ByteView use, TLS inputs and all shared ownership arcs in WebSocket state. Definitions carry the coroutine-free callback and native operation analysis.

sites.label: Synchronous event guard and custom microtask
sites.reason: The guard invokes its borrowed callback immediately. nextTick instead moves an owning callback to the loop and returned headers or errors own their values.

sites.label: Native Socket buffer and callback declarations
sites.reason: The socket owns read storage and makes delivery spans call-scoped. Posted read and event callbacks capture strong owners, and the implementation distinguishes write-queue ownership during cancellation.

sites.label: Receiver and Sender byte and frame interfaces
sites.reason: The receiver copies payloads before emitting and uses short views only during parsing. Sender copies source bytes to an owning frame before the socket write and holds its socket by shared owner.

sites.label: Handshake and cross-file handoff declarations
sites.reason: Connection targets, upgrade bytes and operation handles are retained by the appropriate callback or local caller; response parser views are consumed synchronously.

sites.label: The pending queue is the sole asynchronous write-buffer owner
sites.reason: Its stored data can disappear when shutdown discards the write queue. The handler needs ownership independent of queue membership.

sites.label: WebSocket state retains loop-bound socket members
sites.reason: The WebSocket owns both Sender and Socket across context shutdown if an external owner retains the public handle.

src/rt/websocket_socket.cpp.note: Reviewed plaintext and TLS byte storage, synchronous callback reentrancy, Asio initiation and completion, ordinary close, cancellation, and context shutdown. There are no coroutine bodies, but Asio completions suspend access to the native buffers.

sites.label: Read buffer and held-input delivery
sites.reason: The outstanding Asio read owns Socket and its stable readBuffer_. Deferred held-input delivery removes each entry before dispatch, while native and TLS spans are consumed synchronously.

sites.label: EOF and read-error callbacks
sites.reason: The read handler pins Socket and moves or copies the active callable before invocation. EOF handling checks destroyed_ after emitting end.

sites.label: Closing a WebSocket releases the native write buffer before completion
sites.reason: The queued bytes are the sole buffer owner, and the handler owns Socket without independently pinning the pending entry. Asio requires the storage through completion even when close cancels the operation.

defect.severity: native write-buffer lifetime on WebSocket request paths
interleaving: A send reaches would-block and async_write_some borrows the front item's bytes. Its completion has yet to run.
A normal terminate or loop teardown closes the descriptor and discards the queue before the completion is delivered or destroyed.

sites.label: Write progress, activity and user callbacks
sites.reason: The installed activity handler only refreshes the current handshake timer. User completions run after their queue entry is removed, and onWritten rechecks whether they destroyed Socket.

sites.label: End, destroy and listener release
sites.reason: Scheduled end and close operations own Socket, pending completions move out for one-shot delivery, and close/error use local listener copies before removing stored hooks.

sites.label: TLS setup, certificate views and handshake completion
sites.reason: OpenSSL receives synchronously consumed option storage and owns its BIOs after setup, while callbacks own Tls options and the native receiver is pinned by the handshake caller or read handler.

sites.label: TLS plaintext and ciphertext buffers
sites.reason: The handshake moves the pending plaintext queue out before flushing it, TLS views stay in a synchronous delivery, and owned ciphertext moves into the native write queue.
